name: The five mother sauces
scope: The idea that almost every classic French sauce descends from a handful of 'mother' sauces, each = a liquid + a thickener. T1a: the creamy white sauce in lasagna and mac-and-cheese is milk thickened with a cooked flour-and-butter paste (bechamel). T1b: that flour-cooked-in-fat paste is the thickener under most classic sauces (a roux). T2a: loosen a pale roux with clear chicken or fish stock and you get the 'velvet' sauce (veloute) - stock is the liquid. T2b: cook the roux dark and add brown roasted-bone stock and you get the deep-brown mother sauce (espagnole). T3a: ONE mother sauce is thickened by its main ingredient cooking down, not by roux at all (tomato) - and it's the only one that couldn't exist in France before the Americas. T3b: the fifth mother sauce uses no roux and no long simmer - it's an emulsion held by egg yolk (hollandaise). T4a: stir grated cheese into bechamel and you get the sauce of a gratin (Mornay). T4b: add a tarragon-shallot-vinegar reduction to hollandaise and you get the classic steak sauce (bearnaise). T4c: Escoffier's famous five updated Careme's earlier list by promoting two sauces Careme hadn't ranked as 'mother' (tomato and hollandaise). T5a: the DARKER you cook a roux, the LESS it thickens - toasting breaks the starch, so a near-black gumbo roux is for flavor, not body. T5b: reduce espagnole with more brown stock and it concentrates into the glossy, intense sauce base pros prize (demi-glace).
source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com) checked first per source priority but returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; corroborated via Wikipedia 'Mother sauce' (Careme 4 / Escoffier 5; per-sauce base + thickener table; bechamel=milk+white roux, veloute=clear stock+blond roux, espagnole=brown stock+brown roux, tomate=tomatoes, hollandaise=egg-yolk emulsion). Build-stage primary refs: Escoffier 'Le Guide Culinaire' (1903), McGee 'On Food and Cooking' (roux browning vs thickening power).
framing_note: Keystone French ladder - reveal the SYSTEM (liquid + thickener) not a definition; scene-led ('the creamy sauce in lasagna...'), never 'What is a mother sauce?'. Every answer is a specific sauce, ingredient, or a mechanism fact - never a bare human name; the Careme-vs-Escoffier rung is answered by WHICH SAUCES (tomato/hollandaise) were added, not by the chefs' names. ACCURACY RAIL: tomato is a New World crop, so sauce tomate could only join the French canon AFTER the Columbian Exchange - never imply a medieval French tomato sauce. Dinner-test payoff = T5a (darker roux thickens LESS, the counterintuitive mechanism) and the pair that break the roux pattern (hollandaise=emulsion, tomato=fruit-thickened). Keep all four choices live: don't name the thickener the stem is asking for.

name: Emulsion and hollandaise
scope: The problem: fat and water refuse to mix, yet French cooking is full of sauces that hold them together. T1: a French vinaigrette (oil + vinegar) separates into layers the moment you stop shaking it - oil and water won't stay mixed on their own. T2: the fix is an emulsifier, a peace-broker molecule; in mayonnaise and hollandaise that job is done by EGG YOLK (context: the yolk compound lecithin grabs fat on one end and water on the other). T3: hollandaise is a WARM emulsion of egg yolk + melted butter + lemon; mayonnaise is its COLD cousin - egg yolk + oil, same trick. T4a: push it too hot or add the butter too fast and the sauce 'breaks' - it splits into a greasy, curdled puddle. T4b: the rescue is to start fresh with a NEW egg yolk (or a spoon of water) and slowly whisk the broken sauce back into it. T5a: swap hollandaise's lemon for a reduction of tarragon, shallot and vinegar and you get the classic steak sauce (bearnaise). T5b: beurre blanc holds butter and wine together with NO egg at all - the emulsion is carried by the butter's own milk solids and hard whisking.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403 to automated fetch); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Hollandaise sauce' (egg-yolk lecithin emulsifies immiscible butter + lemon; breaks from excess heat; bearnaise = vinegar/shallot/tarragon/chervil reduction derivative; name = 'Dutch sauce'). Build-stage refs: McGee 'On Food and Cooking' (emulsion mechanism, breaking/repair), Escoffier 'Le Guide Culinaire'.
framing_note: Mechanism flagship - the payoff is understanding WHY fat+water hold, not memorizing a recipe. Scene-led (the vinaigrette that re-separates). Keep 'lecithin' as CONTEXT/distractor only - the tested answer at T2 is 'egg yolk', never the molecule's name (banned-minutiae rule). ACCURACY RAIL: hollandaise is French despite meaning 'Dutch sauce' - don't attribute it to the Netherlands. Dinner-test payoff = T5b (beurre blanc emulsifies with NO egg) as the contrast that proves the concept, plus the practical T4b rescue. All four choices live: at the 'break' rung don't pre-name the cause in the stem.

name: The braise (boeuf bourguignon and coq au vin)
scope: The counterintuitive truth that the cheapest, toughest cuts make the most tender, luxurious dishes - if you braise them. T1: a slow-cooked stew uses the TOUGH, cheap cuts (shoulder, chuck, shank), the opposite of a quick-grilled steak - and they come out meltingly tender. T2a: what braising melts is collagen, the chewy connective tissue, which long moist heat turns into silky gelatin. T2b: boeuf bourguignon is beef braised in RED wine (Burgundy) with a garnish of lardons, mushrooms and pearl onions - red wine is the braising liquid. T3a: coq au vin was invented to rescue an OLD ROOSTER - a bird too tough to roast, braised for hours in wine until tender (the name literally means 'rooster in wine'). T3b: lardons - little strips of cured pork fried to render their fat - build the savory base of both braises. T4a: you SEAR the meat brown first, before any liquid; the browned bits stuck to the pot (the fond) get scraped up by the wine to build deep flavor. T4b: as it cooks the wine doesn't mostly 'tenderize' - it REDUCES, concentrating into the body of the sauce. T5a: despite the name, boeuf BOURGUIGNON isn't an ancient Burgundy peasant dish - it first appears in 1860s Paris cooking; the 'Burgundy' really points to the WINE. T5b: the tale that coq au vin dates to Julius Caesar and the Gauls is just legend - the recipe isn't written down until the early 1900s.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Beef bourguignon' (tough collagen-rich cut braised in red Burgundy + stock; lardons/pearl onion/mushroom garnish; NOT originally a Burgundy regional dish, first documented 1867, Paris-bistro association) and 'Coq au vin' (old mature rooster needs slow braise; Gaul/Caesar origin is undocumented legend, recipe first documented early 20th c.). Build-stage ref: McGee (collagen-to-gelatin at braising temps).
framing_note: Reveal the MECHANISM (collagen -> gelatin) through two flagship dishes; prep-frame voice ('you sear it, then braise it') is fine. Scene-led hook = 'why does a fancy braise start with the CHEAPEST meat?'. ACCURACY RAILS (two myth-busts baked in as payoffs): boeuf bourguignon is not an ancient Burgundian peasant recipe (label the Burgundy link as the WINE), and the coq au vin / Julius Caesar origin is LEGEND. Avoid overstating wine as a tenderizer - the answer is that it reduces into the sauce. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (the old rooster - the name's real reason). No bare human-name answers.

name: Croissant lamination and viennoiserie
scope: The puzzle of how a croissant gets its hundred crackly layers. T1: a croissant's shattering flake comes from folding cold BUTTER into the dough over and over - not from special flour. T2a: each 'turn' (a fold in thirds) multiplies the sheets, building dozens of paper-thin alternating layers of dough and butter (numbers as context only). T2b: in the oven the WATER trapped in the butter flashes to steam and pries the layers apart, puffing them up. T3a: the butter must stay COLD and solid while you fold - if it warms and melts into the dough the layers merge and the pastry bakes dense, not flaky. T3b: unlike puff pastry, croissant dough also contains YEAST, so it rises from fermentation AND flakes from lamination - that's what makes it 'viennoiserie'. T4a: puff pastry (pate feuilletee) is the same lamination but with NO yeast - pure steam-lift, which is why a mille-feuille is crisp-shattery and a croissant is bready-flaky. T4b: the croissant isn't originally French - it descends from the Austrian crescent roll, the kipferl, carried to Paris in the 1800s (the buttery laminated version we know is early-1900s French). T5a: 'mille-feuille' literally means 'a thousand leaves' - the name IS the lamination trick in three words. T5b: you laminate by locking a flat block of butter inside the dough, then rolling and folding to spread it into sheets.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Croissant' (evolved from Austrian kipferl; August Zang's Paris Viennese bakery 1838-39; modern laminated butter croissant early 20th c.; yeast-leavened viennoiserie vs unleavened puff pastry; repeated butter-folding creates the layers) and 'Mille-feuille' (name = 'thousand leaves'). Build-stage ref: McGee (steam lift in lamination).
framing_note: Technique flagship - reveal the MECHANISM (folded butter + steam) and the yeast-vs-none distinction. Scene-led ('why does a croissant SHATTER into flakes?'), never 'What is lamination?'. Prep-frame voice fine. ACCURACY RAIL: the croissant is Austrian-derived (kipferl), and the Marie-Antoinette-invented-the-croissant story is LEGEND - do not present it as fact. Dinner-test payoff = T2b (steam from the butter's water lifts the layers) and T3b (yeast is what separates croissant from puff pastry). Keep 'a thousand leaves' as a wonder-vocab gem, not a numbers question.

name: Stock, fond and mirepoix
scope: The unglamorous pot of bones that classical French cooking is secretly built on. T1: real French cooking starts with a pot of bones and vegetables simmered for hours - the 'stock', whose French name FOND literally means 'foundation'. T2a: the trio of vegetables flavoring almost every French stock and braise is onion, carrot and celery - the mirepoix. T2b: stock gets its body - that lip-sticking richness - from collagen in the bones dissolving into GELATIN. T3a: white stock uses raw bones; brown stock ROASTS the bones first for deeper color and flavor. T3b: you SIMMER a stock, never hard-boil it - boiling churns fat and scum back in and turns it cloudy. T4: boil a brown stock way down and it concentrates into demi-glace, a syrupy, intense sauce base.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Stock (food)' (fond = foundation; fond blanc raw bones + mirepoix of onion/carrot/celery; fond brun = roasted bones; bone collagen -> gelatin gives body; simmer-not-boil for clarity; reduction to demi-glace). Build-stage ref: Escoffier 'Le Guide Culinaire' (stock as the base of all sauces).
framing_note: Foundational technique ladder - reveal WHY stock matters (gelatin body, the base under sauces). Scene-led ('the pot French cooking is secretly built on'). Answers are concrete: the mirepoix trio, gelatin, roasted bones, simmer-not-boil, demi-glace - never a bare definition. ACCURACY RAIL: keep 'fond' meaning literal ('foundation') and don't confuse mirepoix (onion/carrot/celery) with the Cajun 'holy trinity' (onion/celery/bell pepper). Dinner-test payoff = T2b (collagen -> gelatin is what gives stock body). All choices live.

name: Beef Wellington
scope: The showpiece roast wrapped in pastry - and the engineering that keeps the pastry crisp. T1: Beef Wellington wraps a whole beef fillet (tenderloin) in pastry and bakes it - the grandest 'meat in a blanket'. T2a: between the meat and the pastry is a layer of finely chopped mushrooms cooked down dry (duxelles). T2b: the classic wreck is a SOGGY BOTTOM - juices from the meat soaking into the pastry. T3a: the fix is that the duxelles (plus a wrap of prosciutto or a thin crepe) acts as a moisture BARRIER, soaking up meat juices so the pastry stays crisp. T3b: 'en croute' means 'in a crust' - Beef Wellington is essentially the French filet de boeuf en croute under a British name. T4: nobody can actually prove it's named for the Duke of Wellington - food historians think it's a patriotic rebrand of the French en-croute dish.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Beef Wellington' (beef tenderloin + mushroom duxelles + puff pastry; prosciutto wrap retains moisture and prevents soggy pastry; 'presumably' named for Arthur Wellesley but connection unknown; historian Leah Hyslop - patriotic rebrand of filet de boeuf en croute).
framing_note: Dish ladder built around ONE mechanism payoff (the moisture barrier). Scene-led - set the 'soggy bottom' PROBLEM in the stem without revealing the barrier fix (anti-restatement: the player must know the duxelles/prosciutto solves it). ACCURACY RAIL: the Duke-of-Wellington naming is uncertain/unproven - frame T4's answer as the FOOD fact (it's the same dish as French filet de boeuf en croute), not the Duke's name. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (the duxelles moisture barrier). Prep-frame voice fine.

name: The souffle
scope: The dessert-or-dinner that dramatically rises tall then sinks. T1: a souffle's puff comes from air beaten into egg WHITES, gently folded into a flavored base. T2a: in the oven the trapped air expands and moisture turns to steam - together they inflate it and it rises tall. T2b: the name says it all - souffle is French for 'puffed / blown'. T3a: it ALWAYS collapses a few minutes after leaving the oven, because as it cools the air contracts and the structure sinks. T3b: a savory cheese souffle is built on a thick bechamel base, a sweet one on pastry cream or fruit - the base carries flavor, the whites carry the lift. T4: don't open the oven mid-bake - the rush of cool air can make it fall early.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Souffle' (beaten egg whites trap air; heat expands air + converts moisture to steam = rise; cooling contracts them = collapse in 5-10 min; name = past participle of souffler 'to blow/puff/inflate'; savory cheese/vegetable base vs sweet chocolate/fruit).
framing_note: Mechanism ladder - the wonder is the rise-AND-fall. Scene-led ('why does it sink the moment it hits the table?'). Every answer is a concrete cause (beaten whites, expanding air + steam, cooling, the base). Link to the mother-sauce ladder via the bechamel base. ACCURACY RAIL: the collapse is normal physics (cooling contraction), not a 'failed' souffle - don't imply a droop means the cook erred. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (it falls because it cools). Keep all four choices live.

name: Choux pastry (eclairs and cream puffs)
scope: The one dough behind a whole family of hollow French pastries. T1: an eclair or cream puff is HOLLOW inside - that empty dome is the whole point, built to be filled with cream. T2a: choux is the strange dough you cook TWICE - first as a paste on the stovetop, then baked. T2b: it puffs with no yeast and no baking powder - just STEAM from its high water content blowing it up like a balloon. T3a: cooking the flour paste on the stove first gels the starch so it can hold lots of egg and water - and that water is the fuel for the steam. T3b: one dough, a whole family - eclairs, profiteroles, the cheese-puff gougere, the wheel-shaped Paris-Brest, the towering croquembouche.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Choux pastry' (pate a choux; boiled butter+water then flour cooked on stove gels the starch to hold more water, eggs beaten in after; high moisture -> steam puffs it into a hollow shell; products: eclair, profiterole, gougere, croquembouche, Paris-Brest).
framing_note: Reveal the MECHANISM (steam-leavened, no yeast) and the breadth (one dough, many pastries). Scene-led/invert-wonder: lead with the HOLLOW interior as the puzzle, make steam the knowable answer. Prep-frame voice fine. ACCURACY RAIL: choux rises from steam alone - do NOT attribute its lift to yeast (that's croissant) or to baking powder. Dinner-test payoff = T2b (steam from its own water is the leavening). Keep the pastry-family rung as a recognition payoff, all four choices live.

name: Confit and cassoulet
scope: The southwest-French trick of cooking meat IN fat - to eat and to keep. T1: duck confit is duck legs cooked slowly and gently submerged in FAT - not fried, but poached in fat. T2a: it began as PRESERVATION - sealed under a cap of fat, meat keeps for months because oxygen can't reach it. T2b: confit comes from Gascony in southwest France, where cooks prize duck and goose fat the way others use olive oil. T3a: today 'confit' means anything cooked slow-and-low in fat - even garlic confit or tomato confit. T3b: cassoulet is the great bean-and-meat bake of the Languedoc - white beans slow-cooked with duck confit, sausage and pork. T4: cassoulet is named for the cassole, the earthenware pot it bakes in - the dish is named after its dish.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Confit' (duck/goose legs poached low in rendered fat ~<85-90C; fat seals from oxygen once cool = months of storage; specialty of southwest France/Occitania 'confit country'; generalized garlic/onion confit) and 'Cassoulet' (haricot beans + pork/sausage/duck-goose confit; Languedoc - Castelnaudary/Carcassonne/Toulouse; named after the cassole earthenware pot).
framing_note: Reveal an ORIGIN + a preservation MECHANISM. Scene-led ('why cook a duck leg drowned in fat?'). Prep-frame + matter-of-fact meat wording is fine for a kid, never gory. ACCURACY RAIL: modern restaurant 'confit' is often just a cooking method with no preservation - distinguish that from the traditional keep-it-for-months purpose (the answer at T2a is the oxygen seal). Dinner-test payoff = T2a (the fat cap seals out air). Cassole-names-cassoulet is the vocab gem.

name: The French omelette
scope: The two-egg dish chefs use to judge each other - all technique, no browning. T1: a proper French omelette is pale YELLOW, never brown - browning means the pan was too hot. T2a: you keep the eggs moving constantly over gentle heat so the curd stays tiny, soft and creamy. T2b: the French leave the center slightly runny - they call it baveuse. T3a: it's rolled into a neat oval, not folded flat and stuffed like an American diner omelette (which is deliberately browned and filling-heavy). T3b: the world-famous omelette de la Mere Poulard at Mont-Saint-Michel is prized purely for TECHNIQUE - served plain, no fillings.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Omelette' (classic French: butter, gentle heat, constant early stirring, unbrowned, soft interior, rolled oval; American version cooked hotter, browned, folded flat, heavy fillings; omelette de la mere Poulard of Mont-Saint-Michel, 'most famous omelette', served plain).
framing_note: Technique ladder - the wonder is that restraint (no browning, no fillings) is the mark of skill. Scene-led/invert: 'why is a browned omelette the sign of a WORSE cook?'. Prep-frame voice fine. ACCURACY RAIL: keep the French-vs-American contrast honest (pale/rolled/creamy vs browned/folded/stuffed) - neither is 'wrong', they're different dishes. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (rolled and pale, the French signature). 'Baveuse' is the vocab gem. All four choices live.

name: Creme brulee and the custard
scope: The dessert you crack with a spoon. T1: creme brulee's signature is the thin, glassy sugar crust you tap through - made by torching sugar on top until it caramelizes. T2a: the name means 'burnt cream' - the 'burnt' is that caramelized top. T2b: underneath is a custard - cream set with egg YOLKS (no flour) into a silky, wobbly base. T3a: custards bake in a water bath (bain-marie) so gentle, even heat sets them without scrambling the eggs or cracking. T3b: its cousin creme caramel (flan) hides its caramel at the BOTTOM - poured in first so it flips out as a sauce; creme brulee's caramel is torched on top and stays crisp.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Creme brulee' (custard of cream + egg yolks + sugar baked gently in a water bath; torched caramelized sugar crust on top; name = 'burnt cream'; earliest recipe Massialot 1691; distinct from creme caramel/flan where caramel lines the bottom).
framing_note: Reveal a TECHNIQUE (gentle custard-setting) plus a caramelization payoff. Scene-led ('the dessert you crack'). Every answer is concrete (torched sugar, egg yolks, water bath, caramel-on-top vs bottom). ACCURACY RAIL: creme brulee's crust is torched ON TOP and crisp; flan's caramel is at the bottom and saucy - keep the two distinct. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (the bain-marie is WHY custards set smooth, not scrambled). Keep the flan contrast's answer live (caramel position).

name: Caramelized onions and French onion soup
scope: The browning that turns sharp onions sweet - and why it's NOT the same as a seared steak. T1: French onion soup's deep brown color and sweet flavor come from cooking onions LOW and SLOW for a long time, not from any broth coloring. T2a: as onions cook, their natural SUGARS brown - that's caramelization, and it's why long-cooked onions taste sweet instead of sharp. T2b: the soup is finished 'gratinee' - a raft of bread and melted Gruyere browned under the broiler. T3a: caramelization is just SUGAR browning with heat - the same reaction that makes creme brulee's crust and tarte Tatin's color. T3b: caramelization is NOT the Maillard reaction - Maillard needs protein (it's what browns a seared steak or bread crust); caramelization is sugar alone. T4: tarte Tatin is the upside-down apple tart where apples caramelize in butter and sugar in the pan, then the whole thing is flipped - and the 'happy accident' origin story is mostly legend.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'French onion soup' (slowly sauteed/caramelized onions in meat stock, gratineed with bread + cheese; Les Halles Paris, mid-19thc) and 'Tarte Tatin' (apples caramelized in butter+sugar then inverted; Tatin sisters at Lamotte-Beuvron; the accident narrative is largely mythical). Build-stage ref: McGee (caramelization = sugar pyrolysis vs Maillard = amino acid + reducing sugar).
framing_note: Mechanism ladder anchored on a dish - reveal caramelization and, as the sharp payoff, its difference from Maillard. Scene-led ('what makes onion soup sweet and brown?'). ACCURACY RAILS: two, both baked in as payoffs - caramelization (sugar) is distinct from Maillard (needs protein), and the tarte Tatin accident story is LEGEND. Prep-frame voice fine. Dinner-test payoff = T3b (caramelization vs Maillard - a bright 15-year-old can reason it). Keep all four choices live; don't name the reaction in the stem.

name: Ratatouille and Provence
scope: The sun-drenched vegetable stew of southern France - and why it's younger than it looks. T1: ratatouille is a vegetable stew from Provence (around Nice) - eggplant, zucchini, peppers and onion all bound together with tomato. T2a: its Provencal flavor comes from herbes de Provence - thyme, rosemary, bay and the like. T2b: purists cook each vegetable SEPARATELY first, then combine, so each keeps its own texture instead of collapsing into mush. T3a: ratatouille could NOT have existed in old Provence - two of its anchors, tomatoes AND peppers, are New World crops that only reached Europe after Columbus. T3b: the neat fanned-out spiral from the movie isn't classic ratatouille - that's confit byaldi, thin slices baked in a pattern.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Ratatouille' (Provencal/Nicoise stew of tomato, onion, garlic, courgette, aubergine, pepper + Provencal herbs; purist method cooks vegetables separately then combines; no modern-form recipe before late-19th/early-20th c., ingredients arrived post-16th-c Columbian contact; confit byaldi = refined sliced version).
framing_note: Reveal an ORIGIN + a Columbian-Exchange accuracy beat where the FOOD is the anchor. Scene-led ('the stew of a Provencal summer'). ACCURACY RAIL (the payoff): tomatoes and peppers are New World crops - a genuine 'old Provencal' ratatouille is impossible before ~1500, and the named dish is only ~a century old; never imply a medieval ratatouille. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (its two anchors are post-Columbian). Confit byaldi is the wonder gem. All four choices live.

name: French kitchen words on a menu
scope: The French phrases on a menu, each decoded to a real dish or technique (never a bare definition). T1: 'en croute' means the food is baked wrapped in PASTRY - like Beef Wellington. T2a: 'au gratin' means topped with cheese or breadcrumbs and browned under heat - like a bubbling potato gratin (from gratter, 'to scrape'). T2b: 'a la meuniere' means 'in the miller's-wife style' - the fish is dusted in FLOUR and pan-fried in butter (a la = 'in the style of'). T3a: 'flambe' means a splash of brandy or liqueur is set ALIGHT in the pan - the flame is the show, as in crepes Suzette. T3b: the belief that flambeing burns off ALL the alcohol is a myth - only about a quarter actually burns away, so most of it stays.
source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Beef Wellington' (en croute = 'in pastry'), 'Gratin' (browned cheese/breadcrumb crust; from gratter 'to scrape'; e.g. gratin dauphinois), 'Flambe' (ignited spirit ~40% ABV, ~one-quarter of alcohol burns off; crepes Suzette, cherries jubilee, bananas Foster; 'flamed'). Standard culinary usage for 'a la meuniere' (floured + butter-fried, e.g. sole meuniere).
framing_note: Vocabulary ladder made FOOD-ANCHORED - every answer is a dish or a technique, never a dictionary gloss; scene-led ('what does en croute promise on a menu?'). ACCURACY RAIL (the payoff): flambeing does NOT burn off all the alcohol - only ~a quarter goes, most remains; correct the common myth. Dinner-test payoff = T3b (the alcohol mostly stays). Cover the two explicit seed terms (a la, en croute) plus au gratin and flambe. Keep all four choices live - don't let the stem restate the technique the term names.
